IS IT A GOOD IDEA TO GIVE THE FIRST 3 SHOTS OR IJAGES TOGETHER AND CREATE THE SHOT? IN SEEDACNE

Short answer: no, don't do it. Generate them as three separate single-shot clips and cut them together in post.

Here's why, strictly per the Seedance guide and what your storyboard needs.

What "giving 3 images together" would actually mean in Seedance

There are only two modes in the guide that take multiple images, and neither fits what you'd want here:

1. First/Last Frame Pinning — exactly two images, start frame and end frame, and Seedance generates the single continuous motion path between them. This is for morphs, teleports, A→B transitions. If you fed Shot 1's back-running frame as start and Shot 2A's shoe macro as end, the model would invent some warped continuous camera move from one to the other. You'd lose the cuts. You'd lose the editorial rhythm. The runner would morph mid-clip. Wrong tool.

2. Multi-Shot mode with Shot labels — this is the closest to what you might be imagining. You write Shot 1: ... / Shot 2: ... / Shot 2A: ... in one prompt and Seedance generates all three as one output with internal cuts. But — and this is the critical limit from the guide — multi-shot generations cap at 15 seconds total across all shots, and reference images in multi-shot mode don't pin individual shots reliably. The first frame anchors the whole generation, not Shot 2 specifically. You'd get drift.

The guide is also explicit on this: "Spatial continuity breaks on cuts — re-anchor positions after every cut." That re-anchoring needs a fresh reference image per shot. Multi-shot in one generation can't do that.

Why three separate generations is the right call

You already have three precisely-framed reference images. That's gold. The whole point of image-to-video is that the storyboard frame is the locked first frame. If you bundle them, you forfeit that lock on shots 2 and 2A.

Per-shot iteration. If Shot 1 nails it on take 2 but Shot 2A needs four attempts to get the foot strike right, you only re-roll the broken one. In a bundled generation, one bad shot = re-rendering all three, burning credits and time.

Better audio. The guide says diegetic audio is generated natively in the same pass. The audio you want for the back-follow shot (footstrikes + ambient canyon) is different from the audio for the macro (isolated heavy thud). One prompt = one audio bed averaging across all three. Bad outcome.

Consistent identity is solved by the wardrobe lock in your prompts, not by bundling. You're already feeding identical wardrobe descriptions across all three Reference Mode prompts. The runner reads as the same person because you described the same person, not because the model saw three frames at once.

Cleaner cuts. Editors cut on motion and rhythm. Three independent clips give you control over exact in/out points. A single bundled output bakes the cut timing into the generation — and the model picks where to cut, not you.

The right workflow for your first 3 shots

Generate Shot 1 as Reference Mode single-shot using shot_01.png as first frame. 6 seconds. Pick best of 2–3 takes.

Generate Shot 2 as Reference Mode single-shot using shot_02.png as first frame. 6 seconds. Pick best of 2–3 takes.

Generate Shot 2A as Reference Mode single-shot using shot_02A_DETAIL.png as first frame. 5 seconds. Pick best of 2–3 takes.

Cut together in Premiere/Resolve. Match grade across all three (you already specified the same warm-highlight-over-cool-desaturated look in each prompt, so the grading work is minimal).

The one exception worth knowing about

If you wanted Shot 1 → Shot 2 to be a single continuous take with no cut — say, a whip-pan that swings from behind the runner around to face him — then First/Last Frame Pinning would be the right move. You'd feed shot_01.png as <<<image_1>>> and shot_02.png as <<<image_2>>> and write a motion path between them. But your storyboard explicitly cuts between Shot 1 and Shot 2, so this isn't your situation.

Stick with three separate generations. It's slower-feeling but actually faster end-to-end, and you keep full editorial control.

What you need to know before firing this

Reference image limitation in multi-shot. Per the guide, the engine accepts up to 9 reference images, but in multi-shot mode the first frame anchors the whole generation, not individual shots. Hard duration cap is 15 seconds total. Three shots = roughly 5 seconds each. That's tight for a stair descent + handheld follow + street resolution. Anything more breathing-room than that and you're back to single-shot mode.

Re-anchoring after every cut is mandatory. The guide is firm: "Spatial continuity breaks on cuts — re-anchor positions after every cut." So each shot label has to re-state where the runner is, what he's wearing, and what the camera is doing — even though it feels redundant.

What I'm watching for when this comes back

A few things will probably need attention on first generation. Flagging now so you know what to look for:

Identity drift between Shot 3 and Shot 4. This is the single biggest risk. The reference image only anchors Shot 3. If Shot 4's runner looks like a different guy (different face, slightly different tank graphic, wrong hair), that's the model improvising — not your prompt failing. The fix if it happens: drop multi-shot, generate Shot 4 separately as Reference Mode using your shot_04 storyboard frame.

Shot transitions defaulting to crossfade or morph. The guide says cuts re-anchor, but Seedance sometimes interprets shot labels as soft transitions rather than hard cuts. If you see a dissolve between Shot 3 and Shot 4, it's the engine being polite. Your edit can clean this up by trimming the transition frames in post, but ideally the cut is clean from the generation.

Audio continuity across cuts. Diegetic audio in multi-shot mode sometimes blends across shot boundaries instead of cutting with them. The footstrike from Shot 3's concrete should change character on the cut to Shot 4's stone canyon — not crossfade. You may need to replace audio in post regardless.

Timing slip. "(~5s)" is a hint, not a hard frame count. The model might give you 4s + 5s + 6s. Edit accordingly.

My honest recommendation after seeing this

Run this multi-shot generation once and see what comes back. If it's clean, great — you've saved three generation passes. If identity drifts on Shot 4 or the cuts feel soft, fall back to single-shot Reference Mode for these three using your shot_04, shot_05, and whatever frame you have for the street resolution. Multi-shot is a speed play; single-shot is the control play. You'll know within one render which one this sequence needs.
